subject: Pathology
summary: Progesterone receptors are nuclear proteins that mediate progesterone’s effects on target tissues. Their presence or absence in tumors guides prognosis and therapy, especially in breast and endometrial cancers.

sections.p: Progesterone receptors are intracellular proteins that bind progesterone and regulate gene transcription. In pathology, immunohistochemistry (IHC) detects PR expression in tissue sections, reporting percentage of positive tumor cells and staining intensity.
b: IHC uses anti‑PR antibodies; results reported as % positive cells and intensity (0–3+).

t.b: Positive (>1% cells, 1+ or higher) suggests hormone‑responsive disease; negative indicates less likely to respond to hormonal therapy.

sections.p: PR status is not a staging parameter but a prognostic marker. In breast cancer, PR positivity correlates with lower grade, lower proliferation, and better response to endocrine therapy. In endometrial cancer, PR loss associates with higher grade and poorer outcomes.
b: PR+ = favorable prognosis; PR‑ = higher risk of recurrence.

sections.p: Loss of PR expression arises from genetic mutations, promoter methylation, or downstream pathway alterations. In cancers, it reflects dedifferentiation and aggressive biology.
Clinically, PR status itself has no symptoms. Its implications appear when evaluating tumors: PR‑ tumors may present with larger size, higher grade, and earlier metastasis.
b: PR‑ tumors often larger, higher grade, more aggressive.

sections.p: The primary investigation is IHC PR staining. In resource‑limited settings, a simple tissue biopsy with routine H&E can suggest aggressive features, prompting referral for IHC if available.

t.b: Positive indicates potential benefit from endocrine therapy; negative suggests alternative treatments.
Poorly differentiated tumors often lack PR.

sections.p: PR‑ status in breast cancer predicts higher risk of recurrence and metastasis. In endometrial cancer, loss of PR signals aggressive disease and potential for rapid progression.

Treat the underlying cancer per standard guidelines. For PR‑ tumors, endocrine therapy is less effective; focus on chemotherapy, targeted agents, or clinical trials. Supportive care includes monitoring for side effects and disease progression.
b: Use chemotherapy or targeted therapy for PR‑ tumors
Consider clinical trials for novel agents

t.b: PR‑ tumors usually do not respond; use only if PR+.
PR‑ status suggests need for cytotoxic therapy.

sections.p: Regular imaging and tumor marker monitoring per cancer type. Prevention focuses on modifiable risk factors: obesity, hormone replacement therapy, and early detection of precancerous lesions.
b: Annual mammography for breast cancer survivors
Regular pelvic exams for endometrial cancer survivors

sections.p: PR status is distinct from estrogen receptor (ER) status, although they often co‑express. It is also different from HER2/neu overexpression, which indicates a separate pathway.

faq.q: What does a PR‑ tumor mean for treatment?
faq.a: It indicates the tumor is less likely to respond to hormonal therapy, so chemotherapy or targeted agents are preferred.

faq.q: Can PR status change over time?
faq.a: Yes, tumors can lose PR expression after treatment or disease progression, necessitating repeat biopsies.

faq.q: Is PR testing done for all cancers?
faq.a: It is standard for breast and endometrial cancers; other tumors may be tested if hormone responsiveness is suspected.

exam: Explain why PR positivity predicts better response to endocrine therapy in breast cancer.
Describe the implications of PR loss in endometrial carcinoma prognosis.
Outline the steps to obtain and interpret PR IHC results in a resource‑limited setting.
